l, irregular or annualised hours

Workers who leave employment have their annual leave pro-rated based on the time that they spent in work as a proportion of the year. This is calculated based on calendar days in employment, not days spent at work.

Calculating the proportion of a leave year worked is done from the start of the leave year to the end of the worker’s time in employment.

The statutory holiday entitlement for a worker who leaves part-way through a leave year is:

Statutory Holiday Entitlement = 5.6 weeks x proportion of leave year in employment

Example 13

Steve has been working on an irregular hour’s contract for more than a year. His leave year started on 1 January 2019, and he is leaving his role on April 13, 2019.

Between 1 January 2019 and 13 April 2019 there are 103 calendar days. The leave year runs from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2019 so does not include a leap day. This means that Steve has been in employment for 103 out of 365 days in the leave year, or 28.2% of the leave year.

Steve’s holiday entitlement of 5.6 weeks should then be pro-rated based on his time in employment. Therefore, Steve’s holiday entitlement is 28.2% of 5.6 weeks or 1.59 weeks’ annual leave.

4.4 Shift workers

Workers who leave employment have their annual leave pro-rated based on the time that they spent in work as a proportion of the year. This is based on calendar days in employment, not days spent at work.

The legislation does not state how to calculate the full statutory annual leave entitlement for shift workers. In our view, an appropriate practical approach is to make calculations on the basis that shift workers are entitled to 5.6 weeks of their average working week, restricted to 28 days of shifts.

The statutory holiday entitlement for a worker who leaves part-way through a leave year is:

Leave entitlement for full year x Proportion of leave year in employment

This is best calculated in a 3-step method:

Calculate the worker’s full annual leave entitlement

Work out the proportion of the leave year worked

Pro-rate based on the proportion of the year worked

Example 14

Abigail has been working for her current employer for more than a year, working a shift pattern of 7 shifts every 10 days. Her employer’s leave year started on 1 April 2019, and she is leaving her role on 5 August 2019.

Step 1 – Calculate full annual leave entitlement

Abigail’s full statutory annual leave entitlement can be calculated based on Section 1: Days per week.

Abigail’s average working week is calculated as (7 ÷ 10) x 7 = 4.9 shifts per week.

For a full year, Abigail is entitled to the lower of 28 shifts or 5.6 x 4.9 shifts (27.5 shifts). Therefore, Abigail’s full annual leave entitlement is 27.5 shifts.

Step 2 – Calculate proportion of leave year in employment

Between 1 April 2019 and 5 August 2019 there are 127 calendar days. The leave year runs from 1 April 2019 to 31 March 2020, so would include 29 February 2020; a leap day. Therefore, Abigail is in employment for 127 days out of 366 days in the leave year or 34.7% of the leave year.

Step 3 – Pro-rate leave based on the proportion of the leave year worked

Abigail’s leave entitlement in the leave year up until she leaves her job is 34.7% of 27.5 shifts, or 9.6 shifts’ statutory leave.

5. 4. Calculating leave for somebody starting and leaving part-way through a leave year

Workers who are in employment for less than a full leave year have their annual leave governed in 2 ways.

Whilst in employment, the statutory annual leave they can take is accrued monthly as governed by regulation 15A of the Working Time Regulations. Under this regulation workers accrue 1/12th of their total annual leave entitlement on the first day of each month (see Section 2).

When they leave employment, regulation 14 governs the workers’ total statutory annual leave entitlement, and any payment that must be made to a worker in lieu of untaken leave. Regulation 14 calculates leave based on calendar days in employment (not days spent working). This is covered by the calculations in this section which can be used to check that a worker received the statutory minimum annual leave to which they were entitled. Any shortfall should be paid for in lieu of untaken annual leave.

It is important to note that if the leave year is not stipulated in a binding agreement, it starts on the first day of employment. Therefore, it is possible that a leap day (29 February) will be included in the worker’s leave year, even if they are not still in employment over the leap day in question.

5.1 Days worked per week

Statutory annual leave is calculated as:

Leave entitlement for full year x Proportion of leave year in employment

This is calculated in a 3-step method:

Calculate the worker’s full annual leave entitlement

Work out the proportion of the leave year in employment

Pro-rate based on the proportion of the year in employment

Example 15

Gen is working as a summer intern on a 10-week contract. He starts work on Monday 3 June 2019 and finishes 10 weeks later on Friday 9 August. For the duration of his contract, Gen works 5 days a week, and his contract stipulates that his holiday leave year is the calendar year of 2019, that is 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2019.

Step 1

Gen’s full annual leave entitlement is the lower amount of 28 days or 5.6 x 5 days (also 28 days) – see Section 1: Days per week. So his full annual leave entitlement is 28 days.

Step 2

From 3 June 2019 to 9 August 2019 there are 68 days. The leave year runs from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2019 and so does not include a leap day. Therefore, Gen is in employment for 68 days out of 365 days in the leave year or 18.6% of the leave year.

Step 3

Gen’s statutory leave entitlement for his internship is 18.6% of 28 days, or 5.22 days’ statutory leave.

passages.quote:
1. Overview

This guidance explains how to calculate statutory holiday entitlement for workers on different types of contract. It is for use by employers or workers, and accompanies the holiday entitlement calculator.

There is separate guidance on how to calculate the pay that a worker is entitled for their statutory leave entitlement.

1.1 Before you read this guidance

Please first read the holiday entitlement rights information on the basics of how holiday entitlement should be calculated.

This page contains additional detail and complements the holiday entitlement rights guidance. You can use it to help improve your understanding of how to calculate statutory holiday entitlement, but it does not and cannot provide definitive answers to individual queries. Please do not rely upon it in any specific context or as a substitute for seeking advice (legal or otherwise) on a specific circumstance, as each case may be different.

Whether you are a worker or employer, if you are unsure about any aspect of holiday pay entitlement you can contact Acas:

www.acas.org.uk

telephone: 0300 123 1100

textphone: 18001 0300 123 1100

1.2 Holiday entitlement – definitions and working patterns

Holiday legislation grants almost all workers 5.6 weeks paid annual leave a year. This includes:

agency workers

workers with irregular hours

workers on zero-hours contracts

The entitlement is set out in the Working Time Regulations 1998.

A worker continues to accrue holiday entitlement while they are on sick leave, maternity leave, paternity leave, parental leave, shared parental leave and adoption leave (collectively known as ‘statutory leave’). A worker may request holiday at the same time they are on sick leave (but cannot be required to take holiday while on sick leave).

Key terms

the focus is on the legal minimum entitlement of 5.6 weeks’ paid holiday. Many people will have contracts entitling them to additional paid holiday beyond the statutory minimum. Individual contracts should be checked first

‘worker’ refers to all individuals whose employment status is either as a ‘worker’ or an ‘employee’, meaning they are entitled to paid holiday. Find out more about employment status and definitions

it refers solely to the holiday entitlement aspect of paid annual leave. The leave calculated using this guidance must be paid to qualify as part of the statutory 5.6 weeks

leap years and leap days: a leap year is a calendar year containing an additional day added to keep the calendar year synchronised with the astronomical or seasonal year. The additional day, referred to here as a ‘leap day’, is 29 February. The next leap year is 2020 and the next leap day is 29 February 2020

rounding the entitlement up: when calculating the statutory minimum leave entitlement, you must not round the entitlement down (and in certain circumstances it must be rounded up)

exact figures are used in calculations. This means that the final figure may not precisely match the calculation written before it. This approach is taken to mitigate rounding errors; the figures in the written calculation are rounded, but the figures in the actual calculation are not. Answers are rounded up to the same accuracy as in the statutory holiday entitlement calculator (usually available on GOV.UK)

1.3 Different types of working arrangements – definitions

Each main heading of this guidance contains 4 sections, each of which covers the calculations for a different type of working arrangement. We have defined these here, along with definitions of other common terms.

Days worked per week

People with a fixed working pattern involving a set number of days of equal length. Leave can be calculated in days of fixed length.

This can also relate to those who work a pattern of days over a fortnight (for example a 9-day fortnight), as they will have a fixed “average” working week (in this case 4.5 days a week makes up a 9-day fortnight).

Example working patterns:

5 days a week, with each day being 8 hours long

3 days a week, with each day being 6 hours long

9 days every 2 weeks, with each day being 7.5 hours long

Hours worked per week/compressed hours

People contracted to work a set number of hours in a period of time, over days of different lengths. This can be working over a week, a fortnight, or another working pattern.

For some workers who work a fixed number of hours but not the same number of hours each day, or who work part-time, it may be more appropriate to calculate their holiday entitlement in hours. The same may be the case for those who work compressed hours (full-time hours over fewer days).

Example working patterns:

25 hours a week, over 4 days. Monday and Wednesday being 8 hours long, Tuesday and Thursday being 4.5 hours long

40 hours a week, over 5 days. Monday, Wednesday and Thursday being 10 hours long, Tuesday and Friday being 5 hours long

Casual, irregular or annualised hours

People who do not have guaranteed hours or who do not have a regular working pattern. As there is no fixed work pattern on which to base annual leave, the entitlement should instead generally be kept in weeks.

For workers who do not have regular hours, or who are on an annualised hours contract, it may be appropriate to grant paid annual leave to be taken during periods when no work is performed. This depends on the particular circumstances, and employers must ensure workers are able to take their full leave entitlement. This may also include workers on casual employment contracts.

Example working pattern:

a worker on a zero-hours contract who only works when they are offered work by their employer. They are not obligated to accept this work, and have no regular hours.

Annualised hours
